newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Gold Fields not planning forward sales.
newsitem.headline: Gold Fields not planning forward sales.

text.p: Mining house Gold Fields of South Africa Ltd said on Wednesday it had no immediate plans to sell any gold forward despite the current bullion price crisis.

"There wouldn't be a worse time to hedge than right now. Our policy remains not to hedge, but this is not set in concrete," Keith Spencer, general manager of Gold Fields gold operations, told Reuters.

The bullion price fell to its lowest level in 12-years of $313.60 an ounce on July 7 after being hit late last week by news that the Australian central bank had sold 167 tonnes of the metal over the past six months.
In London on Wednesday morning gold was trading at around $316 an ounce.
Gold Fields has said in the past that its shareholders are against hedging and so it will refrain from doing so.
Analysts have said that only South African mines that have locked in gold prices higher than spot levels will be able to weather the current sickly bullion prices.
They cite Anglo American Corp of South Africa Ltd as one mining house with a successful hedging policy that will help it remain relatively unscathed.
Spencer said that previously Gold Fields had managed to reap the benefits of higher spot prices when other mines had locked in prices not as good.
"There have been times when we were unhedged and so we got higher prices than the others," he said.
Spencer said it remained important to take a long-term view.

"We're going through a lot of pain right now but we need to look long-term. There is a lot of negative sentiment about the Australian sales but the fall was triggered by the announcement. The market actually absorbed the gold sales," Spencer said.
Anglo's marketing manager Kelvin Williams on Monday also blamed bullion's slide on the announcement and not the sales.

"The distressing irony in the gold market is that the central bank sales themselves are well managed in a fashion which causes little, if any effect on the gold price. Only after the sales are completed and announced do we see price falling as speculators compete to increase their short positions," he said.
Spencer said physical demand for gold remained "very good" and that the price would recover.

"There is a great deal of physical gold being absorbed into the market. It's just people talking it down. Sooner or later sanity will reign. In the longer term there are good fundamentals," Spencer said.
